questions.stem: A 65-year-old man's serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 1.5 mg/dL over 48 hours. Urine output is 0.4 mL/kg/h for 8 hours. Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. Creatinine rise of 0.5 (>0.3) within 48 hours meets AKI criteria.

Correct. KDIGO stage 1 AKI: serum Cr rise of ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours OR rise to 1.5–1.9× baseline within 7 days, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours. Stage 2: Cr 2.0–2.9× baseline OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h ≥12 h. Stage 3: Cr ≥3× baseline OR Cr ≥4 OR initiation of RRT OR urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h.
Incorrect. Stage 3 requires Cr ≥3× or RRT.
Incorrect. CKD requires >3 months of dysfunction.
Incorrect. The Cr rise is real.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe diarrhea has BUN 60, Cr 2.0 (baseline 1.0), urine Na+ 8, FENa 0.3%, urine osm 580. Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. ATN features FENa >2%, isosthenuric urine, muddy brown casts.

Correct. Pre-renal AKI features: BUN:Cr ratio >20:1 (here 30:1); FENa <1%; urine Na+ <20; urine osm >500 (concentrated); bland urine sediment. Causes: hypovolemia (GI losses, blood loss, sepsis early), reduced effective arterial volume (HF, cirrhosis), renal artery stenosis, drugs (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB). Reversible with restoration of perfusion. If untreated, can progress to ATN.
Incorrect. AIN features WBC casts, eosinophiluria, drug history.
Incorrect. Post-renal would have hydronephrosis.
Incorrect. Acute presentation.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man post-cardiac surgery has Cr 3.2 (baseline 1.0), FENa 4%, urine osm 280. Sediment shows muddy brown granular casts. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect. Pre-renal has FENa <1% and concentrated urine.

Correct. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) features: FENa >2%, isosthenuric urine (osm ~300), muddy brown granular casts (renal tubular epithelial cells), failure of urine concentrating ability. Causes: ischemic (prolonged hypoperfusion, sepsis, post-cardiac surgery, contrast), nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast, cisplatin, amphotericin B), pigment-related (myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobinuria). Recovery typically over 1–3 weeks; some cases progress to CKD.
Incorrect. AIN has WBC casts and eosinophiluria.
Incorrect. Post-renal would have obstruction.
Incorrect. Cardiorenal is a specific HF-AKI interaction.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man received high-dose IV vancomycin and zosyn for MRSA bacteremia. Two weeks later he has Cr 3.5 (baseline 1.0), eosinophiluria, sterile pyuria, and a maculopapular rash. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect. ATN does not feature rash or eosinophiluria.

Correct. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) — drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction with classic features: AKI, RASH, FEVER, EOSINOPHILIA, eosinophiluria (now considered insensitive), WBC casts, sterile pyuria. Common drugs: PPIs (most common cause now), NSAIDs (often without classic triad), antibiotics (β-lactams, sulfonamides, quinolones, vancomycin), allopurinol, 5-aminosalicylates. Treatment: stop offending drug; corticosteroids if no improvement after 5–7 days. Recovery often slow; some progress to CKD.
Incorrect. Pre-renal lacks the inflammatory features.
Incorrect. Post-renal would have obstruction.
Incorrect. GN features RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with BPH has acute oliguria. Cr 3.0 (baseline 1.2). Renal ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. Pre-renal has no obstruction.
Incorrect. ATN does not have hydronephrosis.
Incorrect. AIN does not have hydronephrosis.

Correct. Post-renal AKI from BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION (BPH, urethral stricture) is the most common cause in elderly men. Other causes: bilateral ureteral obstruction (stones, malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, lymph nodes), unilateral obstruction with single functioning kidney. Imaging: renal ultrasound (first-line, shows hydronephrosis), CT for stones or other causes. Treatment: relieve obstruction (Foley catheter for BPH, ureteral stent or nephrostomy for ureteral causes); post-obstructive diuresis monitoring.
Incorrect. GN has hematuria and RBC casts.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient has post-obstructive diuresis after Foley catheter relieved bilateral hydronephrosis from BPH. Urine output is 8 L over 8 hours. Which best characterizes the management?
explanations: Incorrect. Without replacement, severe hypovolemia can develop.
Incorrect. Already diuresing; do not amplify.

Correct. Post-obstructive diuresis can produce massive water and electrolyte losses (Na+, K+, Mg2+, phosphate). Most patients have appropriate physiologic diuresis (release of retained Na+/water); some develop pathologic diuresis (impaired tubular function, urea-driven). Replace 50–75% of urine output with isotonic fluid (often 0.45% NaCl + dextrose), monitor electrolytes (Na+, K+, Mg2+, phos) every 4–6 hours, monitor weight and BP. Avoid full 1:1 replacement (perpetuates polyuria); avoid no replacement (volume depletion).
Incorrect. ACEi is not for post-obstructive management.
Incorrect. Catheter is in place.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF on chronic ACE inhibitor and chronic loop diuretic develops AKI 3 days after starting ibuprofen for back pain. Which mechanism best explains the AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. Direct toxicity is one component but the multidrug interaction is the principal mechanism.

Correct. The 'triple whammy' — NSAID (constricts afferent arteriole by blocking prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation) + ACE inhibitor (dilates efferent arteriole reducing intraglomerular pressure) + diuretic (volume contraction reducing renal perfusion) — combines to reduce GFR. Each individually may be tolerated; together they precipitate AKI especially in elderly, CKD, HF, cirrhosis patients. Recognition: stop NSAID first (most reversible), reduce diuretic, hold ACEi until recovery; optimize volume status.
Incorrect. AIN can occur with NSAIDs but the temporal pattern with ACEi + diuretic suggests hemodynamic AKI.
Incorrect. No CK elevation or muscle injury described.
Incorrect. No GN features.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is found unconscious 24 hours after a drug overdose. CK is 45,000, urine dipstick positive for 'blood' but no RBCs on microscopy. Cr is 4.0 (baseline 1.0). Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. GN features RBC casts.

Correct. Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI from MYOGLOBIN: muscle injury releases myoglobin (and CK, K+, phosphate) into circulation. Myoglobin is filtered, then causes injury via three mechanisms: (1) tubular obstruction (myoglobin casts), (2) direct cytotoxicity, (3) renal vasoconstriction. Diagnostic clue: urine dipstick positive for 'blood' (heme reaction) but NO RBCs on microscopy (myoglobin or hemoglobin without intact cells). Management: aggressive isotonic fluids (target 200–300 mL/h urine output); urinary alkalinization with bicarbonate (pH >6.5) to reduce myoglobin tubular toxicity (controversial); monitor for hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia.
Incorrect. AIN has different sediment.
Incorrect. Pre-renal has different presentation.
Incorrect. No obstruction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with CKD stage 3 (eGFR 35) underwent CT angiography with contrast 48 hours ago. Cr has risen from 1.6 to 2.5. Which best characterizes contrast-induced nephropathy?
choices: Cr peaks at 24 hours then resolves
explanations: Incorrect. Peak is typically 3–5 days, not 24 hours.

Correct. Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) / contrast-associated AKI: rise in Cr within 24–72 hours after IV contrast, peak at 3–5 days, return to baseline by 1–2 weeks in most. Risk factors: pre-existing CKD (especially eGFR <60), diabetes, volume depletion, age, large contrast volume, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, metformin (lactic acidosis risk if AKI develops). Prevention: isotonic IV fluid (NaHCO3 or NS) before/after; lowest contrast volume; iso-osmolar contrast; hold NSAIDs/diuretics around contrast. N-acetylcysteine has fallen out of favor (PRESERVE trial).
Incorrect. Cr rises with CIN.
Incorrect. Effect is real.
Incorrect. Most cases reversible.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed acute leukemia is started on chemotherapy. Within 24 hours she develops AKI with K+ 6.5, phosphate 9.0, uric acid 14, and Ca 7.2. Which best characterizes her AKI?
explanations: Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome — rapid release of intracellular contents from dying tumor cells: K+ (hyperkalemia), phosphate (hyperphosphatemia), nucleic acid breakdown to URIC ACID. Calcium falls (Ca-phosphate precipitation in tissues including kidney). Kidney injury from URIC ACID (uric acid crystals in tubules in acidic urine) and CALCIUM-PHOSPHATE deposition. Most common with hematologic malignancies (leukemia, lymphoma) and bulky tumors after chemotherapy. Prevention: aggressive hydration, allopurinol (reduces new uric acid formation), or rasburicase (degrades existing uric acid — more effective). Treatment: aggressive IV fluids, urinary alkalinization (controversial — promotes Ca-phos precipitation), rasburicase, dialysis for severe.
Incorrect. AIN has different presentation.
Incorrect. Pre-renal does not feature this electrolyte profile.
Incorrect. Post-renal has hydronephrosis.
Incorrect. Membranous is glomerular with proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis and refractory ascites has Cr rising from 1.0 to 2.5 with oliguria. Urine Na+ <10, urine sediment bland, no improvement with volume challenge. Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. Lack of response to volume distinguishes from typical pre-renal.

Correct. Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) — functional renal failure in advanced cirrhosis from intense renal vasoconstriction triggered by splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective arterial volume. Diagnostic features: cirrhosis with portal hypertension; AKI; absence of other identifiable cause; lack of improvement after volume challenge with albumin (1 g/kg up to 100 g for 2 days); bland urine sediment; low urine Na+. Treatment: terlipressin + albumin (FDA approved 2022); norepinephrine alternative; TIPS for selected; liver transplant is definitive. Avoid further nephrotoxins.
Incorrect. ATN typically has muddy brown casts and FENa >2%.
Incorrect. GN features RBC casts.
Incorrect. AIN features pyuria, eosinophiluria, drug history.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with HFrEF and worsening pulmonary edema has rising Cr from 1.4 to 2.5 over 2 days during diuresis. Which best characterizes his AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. ATN typically has muddy brown casts.

Correct. Cardiorenal syndrome — bidirectional dysfunction between heart and kidney. Type 1 (acute cardiorenal): acute HF causes AKI through reduced cardiac output, elevated venous pressure transmitted backward to renal veins (impaired renal perfusion despite low cardiac output), neurohormonal activation, diuretic effects. Type 2: chronic HF causes CKD; Type 3 acute renocardiac (AKI causes acute HF); Type 4 chronic renocardiac; Type 5 secondary cardiorenal (sepsis, etc). Management: balance volume (continue diuresis carefully — venous congestion impairs kidney perfusion), tolerate mild Cr rise with effective decongestion; avoid over-diuresis; ultrafiltration in selected cases.
Incorrect. AIN features eosinophiluria.
Incorrect. No obstruction.
Incorrect. Membranous is glomerular.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with sepsis from pneumonia has Cr 3.0 (baseline 1.0) and oliguria. He has received aggressive fluid resuscitation. Which best characterizes sepsis-related AKI?
explanations: Incorrect. Sepsis-AKI is multifactorial, not pure pre-renal.

Correct. Sepsis is the most common cause of AKI in hospitalized patients. Pathophysiology is multifactorial: hemodynamic (vasodilation, distributive shock), microcirculatory dysfunction (capillary leak, endothelial injury), direct cytokine-mediated tubular injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased oxidative stress. Despite the name 'septic ATN', the histology often shows minimal frank necrosis. Management: source control, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation (avoiding over-resuscitation), vasopressors, vasopressin, supportive care, RRT when indicated.
Incorrect. Direct bacterial invasion is rare.
Incorrect. AIN features different sediment.
Incorrect. Sepsis does not principally cause obstruction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with AKI (Cr 5.0) has K+ 7.0, HCO3− 12, BUN 95, and uremic pericarditis on echo. He is fluid-overloaded with pulmonary edema. Which is the most appropriate management?
explanations: Incorrect. Multiple severe RRT indications exist.

Correct. Indications for RRT in AKI (mnemonic AEIOU): ACIDOSIS (severe metabolic, refractory); ELECTROLYTES (severe hyperkalemia not responsive to medical therapy); INTOXICATIONS (dialyzable toxins — lithium, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, metformin); OVERLOAD (refractory volume overload, especially with pulmonary edema); UREMIA (symptomatic — pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding). This patient has multiple indications. Modalities: intermittent HD, continuous (CRRT — preferred in hemodynamically unstable), peritoneal dialysis. Initiation timing remains debated; most data support no clear benefit to early vs late RRT in AKI without urgent indications.
Incorrect. Some medications (ACEi, NSAIDs) need to be stopped, but RRT is needed.
Incorrect. ACEi is contraindicated in AKI with hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Diuresis alone won't address acidosis, hyperkalemia, uremia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews FENa interpretation. Which best characterizes FENa <1% in AKI?
explanations: Correct. FENa = (UNa × PCr) / (PNa × UCr) × 100. FENa <1% suggests pre-renal physiology — kidney appropriately retaining Na+. FENa >2% suggests intrinsic AKI (ATN, AIN, GN) — kidney unable to reabsorb Na+. FENa 1–2% is intermediate. Caveats: diuretic use makes FENa unreliable (use FE-urea instead, <35% suggests pre-renal); contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis often have low FENa despite intrinsic injury; chronic CKD complicates interpretation; severe hepatorenal syndrome has very low FENa. Always interpret in clinical context.
Incorrect. ATN has high FENa.
Incorrect. AIN typically has variable FENa.
Incorrect. Post-renal has variable FENa.
Incorrect. The Cr rise is real.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on chronic furosemide has AKI with Cr 2.5 (baseline 1.0). FENa is 1.5%. Which alternative test best assesses pre-renal physiology in this diuretic-treated patient?
explanations: Incorrect. FE-Cr is not the standard.

Correct. Diuretics increase urinary Na+ excretion, falsely elevating FENa. FRACTIONAL EXCRETION OF UREA (FE-urea) is more reliable in diuretic-treated patients because urea handling is less affected by loop and thiazide diuretics. FE-urea <35% suggests pre-renal physiology; >50% suggests intrinsic AKI. Calculate similarly to FENa: (Uurea × PCr) / (Purea × UCr) × 100. Caveat: still affected by some conditions (CKD, age).
Incorrect. FENa is unreliable with diuretic.
Incorrect. SG alone is insensitive.
Incorrect. Plasma osm alone does not differentiate.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on a third-line antibiotic for refractory infection has AKI with FENa 3%, sterile pyuria, and WBC casts. Which is the most appropriate first step?
explanations: Incorrect. Continuing the offender worsens AIN.

Correct. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) management: STOP THE OFFENDING DRUG (most important step) — recovery often follows over weeks. Corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks tapered) are considered if no recovery in 5–7 days; benefit is debated but commonly used for severe or refractory cases. Renal biopsy may be needed for confirmation if the diagnosis is unclear or recovery is delayed. Dialysis only if severe AKI with indications.
Incorrect. Dialysis only if specific indications.
Incorrect. Diuresis is not the principal treatment.
Incorrect. AIN is not surgical.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews the timing of AKI biomarkers. Which best characterizes the rise of serum creatinine in AKI?
choices: Cr rises only when AKI is irreversible
Cr is the earliest AKI biomarker
Cr does not change in AKI
explanations: Incorrect. Cr is delayed.

Correct. Serum creatinine rises 24–48 hours after the injury — a fundamental limitation that delays AKI recognition. This delay has prompted research into earlier biomarkers: NGAL (neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin), KIM-1 (kidney injury molecule 1), TIMP-2 × IGFBP-7 (Nephrocheck — FDA-approved for early AKI risk prediction). Cystatin C is an alternative GFR marker less affected by muscle mass. None has fully replaced Cr in clinical practice. Urinary biomarkers may aid early recognition in critically ill patients at risk.
Incorrect. Cr is reversibly elevated in many AKI cases.
Incorrect. Cr is delayed.
Incorrect. Cr does change.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has Cr 2.0 (baseline 1.0). Urine sediment shows muddy brown granular casts. Which best characterizes the implication of these casts?
explanations: Incorrect. GN has RBC casts.

Correct. Muddy brown granular casts (renal tubular epithelial casts) are PATHOGNOMONIC for ATN. Their presence is highly specific. Other findings supporting ATN: tubular epithelial cells, FENa >2%, isosthenuric urine. Sediment findings in other AKI: pre-renal — bland, hyaline casts; AIN — WBCs, eosinophils, WBC casts; GN — RBCs, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts; nephrotic — fatty casts, oval fat bodies, lipid droplets ('Maltese cross' under polarized light); post-renal — variable.
Incorrect. Pre-renal has bland sediment.
Incorrect. AIN has WBC casts.
Incorrect. UTI has WBCs and bacteria but not principally muddy brown casts.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with sustained AKI is being assessed for continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) vs intermittent hemodialysis. Which best characterizes the choice?
choices: CRRT for unstable; IHD for stable
explanations: Incorrect. CRRT is the dialysis modality of choice in many ICU AKI patients.

Correct. CRRT (continuous renal replacement therapy: CVVH, CVVHD, CVVHDF) is preferred in HEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE patients — slower fluid removal and solute clearance over 24 hours minimize hemodynamic shifts. Intermittent HEMODIALYSIS (IHD) is faster (3–4 hours) and preferred in stable patients. SLED (sustained low-efficiency dialysis) is intermediate (8–12 h). Peritoneal dialysis is rarely used in adult AKI. No mortality difference between CRRT and IHD in stable patients (RENAL trial); CRRT preferred for unstable.
Incorrect. IHD is widely used.
Incorrect. They differ.
Incorrect. PD is rarely used in adult AKI.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with crush injuries from a building collapse has Cr 3.5, K+ 6.8, phosphate 8.0, calcium 7.2, and CK 80,000. Which is the most appropriate INITIAL fluid management?
explanations: Incorrect. Restriction worsens rhabdo AKI.

Correct. Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI: aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation (often 1–2 L initial bolus, then 200–500 mL/h) targeting urine output 200–300 mL/h to dilute and clear myoglobin, prevent crystal precipitation. Urinary alkalinization with bicarbonate (pH >6.5) is theoretically protective (reduces myoglobin breakdown to nephrotoxic metabolites and Ca-phosphate precipitation) — practice variable. Watch for hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia (Ca-phos precipitation), compartment syndrome. Mannitol historic; not routinely recommended.
Incorrect. D5W alone does not provide effective volume.
Incorrect. Hypertonic saline not standard.
Incorrect. Mannitol monotherapy is no longer standard.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (Cr 4.5, hematuria, RBC casts, proteinuria 3 g/day). Which best characterizes the initial workup?
explanations: Incorrect. RPGN is a medical, not urologic, emergency.

Correct. RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (RPGN) — clinical syndrome of rapid Cr rise + nephritic sediment (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria). Workup: SEROLOGIES — ANA + dsDNA (lupus), ANCA c/p (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis), anti-GBM (Goodpasture / anti-GBM disease), complement C3/C4 (low in lupus, post-strep, MPGN, cryoglobulinemia), cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C, HIV. URGENT RENAL BIOPSY guides treatment. Treatment by category: Pulse methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide or rituximab for ANCA / lupus / anti-GBM; plasma exchange added in anti-GBM and severe ANCA. Time-critical — irreversible glomerular damage develops within days to weeks.
Incorrect. RPGN is time-critical.
Incorrect. Diuretic challenge is not the principal step.
Incorrect. UTI is not the principal cause.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with AKI on amphotericin B has K+ 2.8, Mg 1.4, and metabolic acidosis. Which best characterizes amphotericin B nephrotoxicity?
choices: ATN with K+/Mg2+ wasting and RTA
Amphotericin B has no renal effect
explanations: Incorrect. Highly nephrotoxic.

Correct. Amphotericin B (especially conventional deoxycholate) is highly nephrotoxic via direct tubular injury — produces ATN with characteristic K+ wasting, Mg2+ wasting, and distal RTA pattern. Liposomal amphotericin (AmBisome) reduces nephrotoxicity. Risk factors: dose, duration, concurrent nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, cyclosporine), volume depletion. Prevention: salt loading (sodium-rich fluids before infusion), use liposomal formulation, monitor electrolytes and renal function. Other tubulotoxic antifungals: voriconazole (less so).
Incorrect. Not principally obstructive.
Incorrect. Not glomerular.
Incorrect. Significant renal toxicity.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has AKI 1 week after starting cefazolin for cellulitis. Cr 2.5, eosinophiluria, fever. Which is the most appropriate management?
explanations: Incorrect. Continuing the offender worsens AIN.

Correct. Drug-induced AIN management: (1) STOP the offending drug — the most important step; (2) supportive care, hydration; (3) CORTICOSTEROIDS (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks tapered) considered if no improvement in 5–7 days. Steroid use is debated (no large RCTs); commonly used for severe or refractory cases. (4) Renal biopsy if diagnosis unclear or recovery delayed. (5) Avoid further nephrotoxins. Recovery often slow (weeks); some progress to CKD.
Incorrect. Vancomycin is also a recognized AIN cause.
Incorrect. Dialysis is not first-line for AIN.
Incorrect. NSAIDs are common AIN cause; should not be added.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews the principal categories of AKI. Which best characterizes the classification?
explanations: Correct. AKI is classically classified into three categories: PRE-RENAL — reduced renal perfusion (hypovolemia, decreased EAV, drugs, RAS); INTRINSIC — direct kidney injury (ATN, AIN, glomerular, vascular); POST-RENAL — obstruction (BPH, stones, malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis). Workup combines history, BUN/Cr, urine sediment, urine indices, and imaging. Each category has different management: pre-renal (restore perfusion), intrinsic (treat underlying), post-renal (relieve obstruction). Most AKI is multifactorial in critical illness.
Incorrect. ATN is only one type.
Incorrect. AKI is acute.
Incorrect. AIN is one type.
Incorrect. Obstructive is one type.
